Have you ever noticed how a traffic light behaves completely differently depending on its current state?
When it is Red cars stop. When it is Green cars go. When it is Yellow cars slow down. Same object. Completely different behavior. All based on its current state.
Now imagine writing this without a pattern:
This works for three states. But what about a vending machine with five states? An order system with eight states? An ATM with ten states?
Every method ends up with the same giant if-else block. Add a new state and you crack open every single method and add another branch. Forget one and you have a bug.
This is exactly what the State Pattern solves.
Instead of one object with a giant if-else, you create a separate class for each state. Each state class knows exactly how to behave. The object simply delegates to whatever state it is currently in.
It is useful when:

["An object behaves differently depending on which state it is in.","You have growing if-else or switch blocks checking state everywhere.","States need to transition automatically based on actions or events."]
items: An object behaves differently depending on which state it is in.
States need to transition automatically based on actions or events.

blocks.content: Let's walk through a real example and see how it works.
1. The Problem: Managing Order States
Imagine you are building an online order management system. On the surface it seems simple place an order, ship it, deliver it.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1778245810404-6ccbda57.png
But the tricky part is that the order's behavior must change depending on what is happening right now. An order can be in only one state at a time:

["PendingState Order placed, waiting for confirmation","ProcessingState Order confirmed, being prepared","ShippedState Order dispatched, out for delivery","DeliveredState Order successfully delivered"]
The system supports these operations:
["confirm() Confirm and start processing the order","ship() Dispatch the order for delivery","deliver() Mark the order as delivered","cancel() Cancel the order"]
Each operation should behave differently based on the current state.

["Calling ship() on a PendingState order should show an error. 
","Calling cancel() on a DeliveredState order should be rejected. 
","Calling confirm() on an already ShippedState order makes no sense.
"]
items: Calling ship() on a PendingState order should show an error.
Calling cancel() on a DeliveredState order should be rejected.
Calling confirm() on an already ShippedState order makes no sense.

blocks.content: The Naive Approach
A common but flawed approach is to manage all state transitions inside one monolithic Order class using if-else blocks.
What's Wrong With This Approach?
1. Cluttered Code All state logic is stuffed into one class. Every method has its own switch block checking the same states over and over. Hard to read, hard to reason about, and easy to break.

2. Hard to Extend Want to add a RefundedState or a ReturnRequestedState? You must open every switch block in every method and add new cases. Every change risks breaking existing logic a direct violation of the Open/Closed Principle.

3. Violates Single Responsibility Order is now responsible for managing state transitions, implementing business rules, and executing state-specific logic all at once. One class doing everything is impossible to test and maintain.
4. Duplicate Logic The same state checks appear in every method. If a rule changes for SHIPPED state, you have to find and update it in four different places.
What We Really Need

We need to encapsulate the behavior of each state into its own class so the Order can simply delegate to its current state object instead of managing everything internally. This would let us avoid switch madness, add new states without touching existing code, and keep each state's logic isolated and independently testable.
This is exactly what the State Pattern enables.
2. The State Pattern

The State Pattern allows an object the Context to alter its behavior when its internal state changes. The object appears to change its class because its behavior is now delegated to a different state object.
Two characteristics define it:

1. Encapsulation of state-specific behavior Each state gets its own class. All the logic for "what happens when an order is pending and someone tries to ship it" lives in the PendingState class not buried in a switch statement somewhere.

2. State-driven transitions State objects themselves decide when and how to move to the next state. The context does not manage transitions through conditionals. It just delegates to the current state and the state handles the rest.

Real-World Analogy

Think about a traffic light.

Red means stop. Yellow means slow down. 

Green means go. Each state knows exactly what it does and when to hand off to the next one. 

Red knows it becomes green. 

Green knows it becomes yellow. The traffic light itself just follows whichever state is currently active.

That is exactly how the State Pattern works the context delegates to the current state, and each state manages its own behavior and transitions.
blocks.title: Note

blocks.content: https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1778245810721-d32983fd.png
The Three Participants

State Interface OrderState Declares the methods that correspond to every action the context supports confirm(), ship(), deliver(), cancel(). Every concrete state must implement all of them. The interface passes the Order context as a parameter so states can trigger transitions by calling order.setState().

Concrete States PendingState, ProcessingState, ShippedState, DeliveredState Each implements OrderState with behavior specific to that state. When an action should move the order forward, the concrete state creates the next state and sets it on the context. No switch blocks. No if-else chains.

Context Order The class clients interact with. It holds a reference to the current OrderState object and delegates every operation to it. It never checks which state it is in it just passes the call through and trusts the state to handle it.
3. How It Works
The State workflow follows a delegation and transition cycle:
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1778245811019-60f0a527.png
Step 1 The context starts with an initial state PendingState.
Step 2 The client calls an action on the context order.confirm().
Step 3 The context delegates the call to the current state currentState.confirm(this).
Step 4 The state performs its logic. If the action triggers a transition, the state creates a new state object and calls order.setState(newState).
Step 5 The next time the client calls an action, the context delegates to the new state which behaves completely differently.
4. Implementing State Pattern
Instead of hardcoding state transitions into one monolithic class, we apply the State Pattern to separate concerns and make the order system easy to manage and extend.
State Diagram
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1778245811753-2418cd86.png
Step 1: Define the State Interface
Every method takes the Order context as a parameter. This allows each state to read order data and trigger transitions by calling order.setState(...).
Step 2: Implement Concrete State Classes
PendingState Order is placed and waiting for confirmation. Only confirm() and cancel() are valid here.
ProcessingState Order confirmed and being prepared. Can be shipped or cancelled.
ShippedState Order dispatched. Can only be delivered. Cannot be cancelled.
DeliveredState Order complete. No further actions allowed.
CancelledState Order cancelled. No further actions allowed.
Step 3: Implement the Context
Order holds a reference to the current state and delegates every operation to it.
Step 4: Client Code
Output

Order ORD-001 created. State: Pending

--- Normal Flow ---
Cannot ship. Order not confirmed yet.
Order ORD-001 confirmed. Now processing.
Order ORD-001 shipped!
Cannot cancel. Order already shipped.
Order ORD-001 delivered successfully!
Cannot cancel. Order already delivered.

--- Cancel Flow ---
Order ORD-002 created. State: Pending
Order ORD-002 confirmed. Now processing.
Order ORD-002 cancelled during processing.
Order is cancelled. Cannot ship.

blocks.content: By using the State Pattern we transformed a rigid condition-heavy implementation into a clean flexible architecture. Each state class knows exactly what it allows and what it rejects. Adding a new state like ReturnRequestedState means creating one new class that implements OrderState no existing state classes or the Order context need to change.

https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1778245811887-099212da.png
